name: Emergency Operations Center
summary_en: San Francisco spent decades looking for somewhere to run an emergency from. A 1993 planning background report recalls that in 1974 the Emergency Operations Center sat at the Youth Guidance Center on Woodside Avenue and was considered inadequate, and describes the search for a site on which to build a new one; a full feasibility study had already been commissioned in 1978 by the Bureau of Architecture and the Mayor's Office of Emergency Services from Reid & Tarics Associates with Parsons Brinckerhoff. Meanwhile the city practised in the building it had — the after-action report on the 1980 Cal Medex earthquake medical exercise devotes a section to operations at the centre, down to meetings with the Department of Electricity about its radio equipment. The centre now stands at 1011 Turk Street. The city's guidebook for new department heads sets out how it works: the Office of Emergency Services maintains it, any department head with emergency responsibilities may request its activation, departments must pre-identify enough staff to run two twelve-hour shifts, and if the main centre is unavailable the alternate is Room 300 at the Moscone Center. Its limits are on the record too: a Civil Grand Jury report notes the first mass-scale activation came on 11 September 2001, and that because space there is limited, supervisors were advised to work through the Mayor's legislative liaison rather than report to it. The building keeps being rebuilt around its function — two storeys of office at $12 million in 1997, a $4 million remodel of the second-floor dispatch area in 2022, and a $3 million replacement of its electrical distribution filed with a sequencing plan to keep the facility operational throughout the work.

At the community level, 911 public dispatchers, fire departments, and law enforcement officials provided the first line of response. City and county emergency operations centers were activated to provide direction and control and to initiate response and recovery procedures. The state Office of Emergency Services (OES) activated the regional emergency operations center in Pleasant Hill, then transferred regional direction and control to the state operations center in Sacramento. Following the earthquake, state officials received and processed requests for resources, coordinated state and local activities, provided damage assessment reports, and released public information.

The fourth background report was Emergency Operations Center. It describes City efforts to establish a new Emergency Operations Center (EOC). In 1974 the EOC was located at the Youth Guidance Center on Woodside Avenue near Twin Peaks. It was considered inadequate. The background report describes the search for a new site for the construction of an up-to-date EOC, proposals that had been made, and the difficulty of securing funding. It also puts forth the concept, which has since been adopted by the City, that in place of an EOC, an Emergency Coordination Center (ECC) could link the City's departmental emergency systems. This paper resulted in a policy of the Community Safety Element to "Establish and maintain an adequate Emergency Operations Center", (Objective 3, policy 4). The fifth background report was Emergency Operations Plan. It describes the governmental response structure for a disaster.
